title: Passover: as if you left (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5)
hook: in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dayenu, fifteen gifts counted one by one. Your line was it would have been enough. Today, the line that makes the whole seder personal.

An anniversary looks back. A national holiday remembers founders long gone. You honor them, but you weren't there. The seder could work the same way: here's what happened to our ancestors, pass the matzah. But a sentence in the Mishnah, read aloud at the seder, refuses to let the story stay in the past tense. It doesn't ask you to remember the Exodus. It asks for something much stranger.
screen: `ANNIVERSARIES LOOK BACK.` → `YOU WEREN'T THERE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT REFUSES.`

segments.voice: At the end of the tractate on Passover, the Mishnah gives Rabban Gamliel's rule: whoever hasn't explained three things at the seder, the Passover offering, matzah and bitter herbs, hasn't fulfilled the duty of the night. Then: in every generation, a person is obligated to see himself as if he himself came out of Egypt. Not our ancestors. Me. The proof is the verse from two days ago, in the old Jewish translation: "It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." The verse speaks in the first person to people who were never slaves. Maimonides, in his version of this law, uses a slightly different word: a person must show himself as if he left. Show, not just see. That's why, he says, people recline at the seder, like free people at a banquet, and drink the cups. The body acts it out. And the Mishnah draws a conclusion: because we came out, we're obligated to thank and praise God. Then the seder breaks into the Psalms of praise. Remembering turns into gratitude, and gratitude into song. One more layer, a wordplay Hasidic teachers used. The Hebrew name for Egypt, Mitzrayim, sounds like meitzarim: narrow places, tight straits. So every person, they taught, has an Egypt, a narrow place they've been held. The seder asks each one to stand in the doorway of their own leaving, every year.
screen: `RABBAN GAMLIEL'S THREE THINGS.` · `IN EVERY GENERATION, AS IF YOU.` · `SEE IT, AND SHOW IT.` · `MITZRAYIM: THE NARROW PLACE.` · then, large: `AS IF YOU LEFT.`

segments.voice: Sit back, the way someone free would sit, and think of a narrow place you've been in: a job, an illness, a fear, a season when the walls felt close. Picture the moment you stepped out, or the step you hope to take, and let your shoulders open. You don't have to be fully out; just stand in the doorway for a moment, as if you left.
Passover. The festival of leaving Egypt, told in the first person, as if you yourself left. Today's word.
Your line: as if you left. The story is told in the first person, every year. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At the seder, the Haggadah reads the Mishnah's line that in every generation each person must see themselves as if they left Egypt; people recline and drink four cups as free people, and then sing the Psalms of Hallel.
